proposal.description_long: President Donald Trump issued an executive order on policing on April 28, 2025. Human Rights Watch’s May 1 analysis said the order would increase military weaponry available to police, expand prison capacity and enhance legal protections for law-enforcement officers’ aggressive actions. HRW argued that these provisions risked expanding mass incarceration and reducing federal oversight and consequences for rights violations. The organization also raised concern about deploying military personnel in domestic law-enforcement roles and prosecuting local officials who opposed the administration’s policies. These statements are HRW’s assessment of the order and its likely consequences. They support describing an advocacy group’s warning about policing powers and accountability. The article does not document the original long description’s specific claims that officials used “quality of life” enforcement to suppress dissent, coordinated prosecutions of demonstrators, or threatened universities with funding cuts over student protests. Nor does a warning about domestic military deployment prove a protest-specific deployment. The corrected title and account therefore focus on the real order and HRW’s stated concerns, keeping the distinction between the policy provisions and the organization’s analysis of their risks.

proposal.title: Alnur Mussayev Claimed Trump Was Recruited by the KGB in 1987
proposal.description_short: Former Kazakh security official Alnur Mussayev alleged Trump was recruited by the KGB; reporting found no corroborating evidence.
proposal.description_medium: In a February 2025 Facebook post, Alnur Mussayev, a former head of Kazakhstan’s security service and former Soviet security official, claimed that the KGB recruited Donald Trump in 1987 under the name “Krasnov.” The Hill and Snopes reported the allegation but found no documentary or other corroborating evidence. proposal.description_long: The February 2025 claim that Donald Trump had been recruited by the Soviet KGB came from Alnur Mussayev, a former head of Kazakhstan’s security service who said he had served in the KGB’s Sixth Directorate. In a Facebook post, Mussayev asserted that the agency recruited a 40-year-old American businessman in 1987 and assigned him the name “Krasnov.” The Hill analyzed the allegation, while Snopes reviewed the post and the available reporting. Neither source produced documentary evidence that Trump was recruited. Snopes noted that Mussayev’s post did not make clear whether he personally carried out a recruitment or was repeating information, and that the claim’s timing did not align with accounts of Mussayev’s documented career. The supplied sources therefore support reporting that Mussayev made the allegation, not the allegation as a proven fact. The prior title incorrectly called him a former KGB chief and stated recruitment as fact. This replacement identifies the speaker and frames the claim as an uncorroborated allegation.

proposal.description_medium: An Associated Press report published March 2, 2026, said Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty’s office was investigating 17 cases involving federal officers during Operation Metro Surge. The reported examples included a January 21 incident in which Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino allegedly threw a smoke canister at protesters, and a January 7 arrest near a high school during which federal officers allegedly deployed chemical irritants while students and staff were nearby. Moriarty said the office was collecting evidence and was prepared for a legal fight.
proposal.description_long: An Associated Press report published March 2, 2026, said Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty’s office was investigating 17 cases involving federal officers during Operation Metro Surge. The reported examples included a January 21 incident in which Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino allegedly threw a smoke canister at protesters, and a January 7 arrest near a high school during which federal officers allegedly deployed chemical irritants while students and staff were nearby. Moriarty said the office was collecting evidence and was prepared for a legal fight. DHS responded that immigration enforcement is a federal responsibility and that states cannot prosecute federal officers acting within their duties. The report also described an evidence portal through which people could submit photos, videos and eyewitness accounts from the operation. At the time of publication, the investigation was ongoing; the story did not report charges or a final court decision on immunity. It documents a state-federal dispute over investigating alleged conduct during an enforcement operation. It does not connect the inquiry to a particular Trump directive or prove that a general enforcement doctrine caused it.

proposal.title: Epstein’s Intercontinental Assets Group and a 1982 Oil-Investment Dispute
proposal.description_short: Vanity Fair reported that Epstein’s IAG handled asset-recovery work and received a 1982 oil investment that became the subject of a dispute.
proposal.description_medium: A 2003 Vanity Fair profile describes Intercontinental Assets Group (IAG), Jeffrey Epstein’s early consulting firm. In a 1989 deposition, Epstein said most of his work involved helping clients recover money from fraudulent brokers and lawyers. The article also reports that Michael Stroll invested $450,000 with IAG in 1982 for an oil venture and later sued over the investment. The supplied evidence does not connect IAG to Trump, Robert Maxwell, Semion Mogilevich, Mossad, or the CIA.
proposal.description_long: A 2003 Vanity Fair profile describes Jeffrey Epstein’s early consulting company, Intercontinental Assets Group (IAG), and a dispute involving one of its investors. The article reports that Epstein testified in a 1989 deposition that he spent about 80 percent of his time helping clients recover money from fraudulent brokers and lawyers. It also recounts a lawsuit by Michael Stroll, a former Williams Electronics executive: Stroll invested $450,000 with IAG in 1982, Epstein put the money into oil, and Stroll later sought repayment. Vanity Fair reports that Stroll received only $10,000 before litigation, while Epstein offered a different explanation for that payment. This supports a focused account of IAG’s stated consulting work and a documented investor dispute. The source does not substantiate the original title’s claims connecting Epstein’s firm to Donald Trump, Robert Maxwell, Semion Mogilevich, Mossad, or the CIA. Those claims should remain out of the entry unless each is supported by specific reliable records.

proposal.title: Trump Sold Palm Beach Estate to Rybolovlev for $95 Million in 2008
proposal.description_short: Property records cited by The Washington Post show Trump bought the Palm Beach estate for $41.4 million in 2004 and sold it for $95 million in 2008.
proposal.description_medium: The Washington Post Fact Checker cited property records showing Trump bought a Palm Beach mansion for $41.4 million in 2004 and sold it to Dmitry Rybolovlev for $95 million in 2008. That is a nominal price difference of about $53.6 million, not proof of a $40 million premium over market value. The linked article provides no comparable-sales analysis, appraisal, or evidence of a payment arrangement. The description reports the transaction and leaves valuation and motive claims out.
